62def5aec815.label: The Tree of Jesse — Victor of Crete, 1674
62def5aec815.title: Victor (iconographer) Tree of Jesse
62def5aec815.read: The Tree of Jesse — the icon the Church paints for Christ’s genealogy. Jesse, the father of David, sleeps at the root; from his side a vine rises bearing the kings and prophets of Israel on its branches, each with a scroll of his own prophecy; and at the summit sits the Theotokos with the Child. Matthew’s forty-two generations are here made visible as one living plant, and Isaiah’s word is fulfilled: there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse.
hot: The Theotokos and the Child
The whole tree grows toward this. She is the flower of the root of Jesse, and the Child in her lap is the fruit for which every branch below was grown.
Jesse asleep at the root
He lies at the foot of the icon, asleep, unaware of what will grow out of him — as the generations of the genealogy were unaware.
The kings crowned above
David and the kings of Judah are painted crowned in the upper branches. Matthew’s first fourteen generations run from Abraham to David, the second from David to the Exile.
The prophets with scrolls
Each prophet holds the words by which he foretold the Child. The genealogy is a list of names in the text and a chorus of voices in the icon.

97ae5ddb1d89.label: The Adoration of the Magi — Monreale, 12th c.
97ae5ddb1d89.title: Cathedral (Monreale) - North arch of transept - Adoration by the Magi
97ae5ddb1d89.read: A twelfth-century mosaic from Monreale in Sicily, worked by Byzantine craftsmen for a Norman king — Eastern iconography in a Western church. The Magi approach the Theotokos enthroned with the Child, offering gold, frankincense and myrrh. The Fathers read the three gifts as a confession: gold to a king, incense to God, myrrh to one who will die and be buried.

ffe73c2bdb6a.label: The Flight into Egypt — Menologion of Basil II, c. 1000
ffe73c2bdb6a.title: Menologion of Basil II - Flight into Egypt
ffe73c2bdb6a.artist: Authors of Menologion of Basil II (circa 985 AC, Constantinople), Byzantine manuscript illuminators[1]: Pantoleon with G
ffe73c2bdb6a.read: A miniature from the Menologion of Basil II, made in Constantinople about the year 1000 — one of the great illuminated books of Byzantium. Joseph leads the ass on which the Theotokos carries the Child out of the land of Israel by night. The icon is quiet and small: the Lord of all is a refugee on a borrowed animal.

ce97ce9df2bc.label: The Holy Innocents — Ionian school, 17th c.
ce97ce9df2bc.title: Massacre of the Innocents (Ionian, 17th c., Byzantine museum)
ce97ce9df2bc.read: A seventeenth-century icon of the Ionian school. The Church commemorates the fourteen thousand Holy Innocents on the 29th of December, four days after the Nativity, and counts them the first martyrs — children who bore witness by dying for Christ before they could speak. Rachel weeping for her children stands in the icon for every mother of them.

0357a9bcae79.label: Christ with St John the Forerunner — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
0357a9bcae79.title: Christos Prodomo Dionysiou
0357a9bcae79.read: Christ enthroned with St John the Forerunner — the Athonite version of the Deesis, in which the Forerunner stands as intercessor beside the Lord. He is painted gaunt and wild-haired, holding a scroll with his own preaching. He is the last of the prophets and the first to point: Behold the Lamb of God.

d4064896388c.label: The Theophany — Ohrid, early 14th c.
d4064896388c.title: Baptism of Christ, Early XIV Century, St Mary Perivleptos Church, Ohrid Icon Gallery
d4064896388c.read: The Theophany — the manifestation of the Holy Trinity at the Jordan. Christ stands naked in the water as one condemned, the Forerunner laying his hand on his head, angels waiting on the far bank with cloths in veiled hands. The Father’s voice comes from above and the Spirit descends: this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
hot: Christ in the Jordan
He stands in the water as in a grave; the river is painted rising round him like a dark tomb. He is baptised not to be cleansed but to cleanse the waters, and through them the world.
St John the Forerunner
He stretches out his hand with fear, having said, I have need to be baptized of thee. The axe often lies at the root of a tree beside him — his own preaching of repentance.
The angels with veiled hands
They stand ready with the garments, their hands covered as servants approach a king. Even the bodiless powers do not touch the mystery bare-handed.
The ray from heaven
A single ray descends to Christ’s head. The Father speaks and the Spirit comes: the Trinity is manifest, which is why the feast is called Theophany and not merely the Baptism.

1c6df2ef1f9b.label: The Temptation of Christ — Monreale, 12th c.
1c6df2ef1f9b.title: Christ's temptation (Monreale)
1c6df2ef1f9b.read: The Temptation in the wilderness, from Monreale. The Latin inscription carries the devil’s words: If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread. The tempter is painted as a dark winged figure — a fallen angel, not a beast: the temptations of Christ are addressed to the mind, and are answered each time out of Deuteronomy.

d327dedf9c14.label: Christ the Teacher — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
d327dedf9c14.title: Christos Didaskon Dionysiou
d327dedf9c14.read: Christ the Teacher, enthroned and expounding — the image the Church sets over the discourses. Orthodox iconography does not usually illustrate the parables as scenes; it paints instead the One who speaks them, seated in the teacher’s place with the elders listening. What matters in a parable is not the anecdote but the mouth it comes from.
hot: Christ enthroned as Teacher
He sits, as a teacher sat in the synagogue, and his right hand is raised in the gesture of speech that is also the gesture of blessing: in him the two are the same act.
The listeners
The elders and scribes are painted attentive and seated at a lower level. They hear the same words as the disciples; hearing is not yet understanding.
The inscription
The Greek titulus above names the scene — Christ teaching. Every Orthodox icon carries its name written on it: the image is never left to the viewer’s guess.

c4d2c9bb6006.label: Christ with the Apostles — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
c4d2c9bb6006.title: Christos Apostolois Dionysiou
c4d2c9bb6006.read: Christ standing among the apostles, both hands outstretched toward the two ranks of them. It is the image the Church uses for the moments when the Lord turns aside from the crowds to instruct, warn or send out the Twelve — including his last word on the mountain in Galilee: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations.
hot: Christ sending
He stands on a footstool with both arms open. The whole composition moves outward from him toward the edges of the panel — the icon of a mission, not of a conversation.
The apostles on his right
They are painted as a close rank of haloed heads, indistinguishable in glory. In Orthodox iconography the Twelve are a body before they are individuals.
The apostles on his left
Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. The apostles are turned outward, already leaving the frame.

305d7ea4cbf0.label: Christ Healing the Multitudes — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
305d7ea4cbf0.title: Iomenos Asthenoun tas apo Poikilon noson
305d7ea4cbf0.read: Christ healing those sick of divers diseases — an Athonite fresco from the katholikon of Dionysiou on Mount Athos, painted in 1547 by a master of the Cretan school. The crowd presses in from every side and Christ reaches into it. Matthew closes chapter 4 with exactly this summary of the whole Galilean ministry.

2b3d17a3e3ad.label: The Commandments of the Beatitudes — Russian icon
2b3d17a3e3ad.title: IkonaZapovediBlazhenGIM
2b3d17a3e3ad.read: A Russian icon of the Commandments of the Beatitudes: each of the nine blessings of Matthew 5 is given its own scene, so that the reader sees what poverty of spirit, mourning, meekness, hunger for righteousness, mercy, purity of heart, peacemaking and persecution actually look like when lived. The Beatitudes are not painted as sentences but as ways of life, which is exactly how the Fathers read them.

863c2ce2d7b8.label: Christ Enthroned — Langadas, Greece, 19th c.
863c2ce2d7b8.title: 105 Christ Enthroned Icon from Saint Paraskevi Church in Langadas
863c2ce2d7b8.read: Christ enthroned, from the icon collection of St Paraskevi in Langadas, northern Greece. He holds the open book — the Gospel is not an object he carries but the word he is — and blesses with the other hand. Where the Church has no narrative icon of a teaching, this is the icon she sets over it.

f53e17ad7406.label: The Cleansing of the Leper — Monreale, 12th c.
f53e17ad7406.title: Christ cleans leper man
f53e17ad7406.read: The cleansing of the leper, from the Monreale mosaics. The Latin above carries the leper’s own words: Thou canst make me clean. What the icon shows and the law forbade is the touch: Jesus put forth his hand and touched him. Contact with a leper made a man unclean; here the current runs the other way.

0336507c47db.label: Christ and the Centurion — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
0336507c47db.title: Iomenos Gon Ekatonarchou Dionysiou
0336507c47db.read: Christ and the centurion, from Dionysiou on Mount Athos. The soldier kneels or stands at a distance, and the servant lies on a bed behind him. His words are said at every Orthodox Liturgy before communion, in the priest’s prayer: I am not worthy that thou shouldest enter under my roof.

e3ab29e84a86.label: Healing of Peter’s Mother-in-law — Monreale, 12th c.
e3ab29e84a86.title: Monreale - Jesus heals Simon's mother in law
e3ab29e84a86.read: Peter’s mother-in-law, healed of a fever, from Monreale. Christ takes her hand and raises her; the Latin names the fever. The detail the icon preserves is what she did next: she arose, and ministered unto them. Healing in the Gospels is never an end in itself.

1a57d2deda4b.label: Christ Stilling the Storm — Gračanica, 14th c.
1a57d2deda4b.title: Hrist utišava buru na moru, manastir Gračanica
1a57d2deda4b.read: Christ stilling the storm, a fresco from the monastery of Gračanica in Kosovo, built by King Milutin in 1321. The boat rides waves painted as hard scrolling ridges, the disciples crowd toward the stern, and Christ rebukes the sea. Byzantine painting shows water as pattern rather than motion — what is dangerous is not the wave but the fear.

c5a887002f86.label: The Gadarene Demoniacs — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
c5a887002f86.title: Christos Iomenos Daimonon Takophon Dionysiou
c5a887002f86.read: The healing of the demoniacs among the tombs — the Gadarenes of Matthew 8, whom Mark and Luke reduce to one. Athos, Dionysiou, 1547. The men come out of the rock-cut graves; the swine run to the sea. The icon keeps the strangeness of the story rather than tidying it.

b6218c06f8f4.label: The Healing of the Paralytic — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
b6218c06f8f4.title: Christos Iomenos Paralyton Dionysiou
b6218c06f8f4.read: The healing of the paralytic, from Dionysiou. The man is shown twice in the same frame — lying before Christ and walking away with his bed on his shoulder. Byzantine icons often paint two moments together, because the icon is not a photograph of an instant but the whole event held still.

809e4f434700.label: St Matthew the Apostle — Langadas, Greece, 19th c.
809e4f434700.title: 090 Mathew the Apostle Icon from Saint Paraskevi Church in Langadas
809e4f434700.read: St Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist — the publican whose calling this passage records, and the writer of this Gospel. He is painted with the book he wrote. The Church keeps his feast on the 16th of November, and reads at it the very verses in which Christ said to him, Follow me.

e74e957600c1.label: The Daughter of Jairus — Monreale, 12th c.
e74e957600c1.title: Daughter of the head of synagogue is resurrected by Christ
e74e957600c1.read: The raising of Jairus’s daughter, from Monreale. Christ takes the girl by the hand on her bed while the mourners stand by — the minstrels and the noisy crowd Matthew mentions, put outside before the miracle. The maid is not awakened but raised: the Greek word is the one used of the Resurrection.

33237ce33d7b.label: The Healing of the Blind — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
33237ce33d7b.title: Christos Iomenos Typhlon
33237ce33d7b.read: Christ healing the blind, Dionysiou, Athos. He touches their eyes with his fingers. In Orthodox iconography every figure has enormous eyes, because the icon is about seeing; the healing of blindness is therefore also a picture of what the icon itself is for.

486477b98e70.label: Christ Casting Out a Devil — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
486477b98e70.title: Iomenos Daimonizomenon Dionysiou
486477b98e70.read: Christ delivering one possessed by a devil — Dionysiou, Athos. The demon is painted small and dark, leaving the man’s mouth or head, and Christ commands with a gesture rather than a struggle. Orthodox iconography gives evil no grandeur: it is shown as small, black and outmatched.

ae630c177c4b.label: The Synaxis of the Twelve Apostles — Constantinople, early 14th c.
ae630c177c4b.title: Synaxis of the Twelve Apostles by Constantinople master (early 14th c., Pushkin museum)
ae630c177c4b.read: The Synaxis of the Twelve Apostles — a Constantinopolitan panel of the early fourteenth century. The Twelve stand together as one assembly, and the Church keeps their common feast on the 30th of June, the day after Peter and Paul. Matthew 10 is where they are first named and first sent.
hot: The inscription
The Greek title across the top reads: The Synaxis of the Twelve Apostles. Their names follow, as Matthew lists them.
The chief apostles in front
Peter and Paul are set forward. Paul is included though he was not of the Twelve — the Church counts the apostolate by calling, not by chronology.
The rank behind
The rest stand shoulder to shoulder, each with the scroll or book of his preaching. Freely ye have received, freely give.

0816dc776ae6.label: The Twelve Apostles — Greek, late Byzantine, early 14th c.
0816dc776ae6.title: The Twelve Apostles, with later gilding, Greek, Late Byzantine, early 1300s, tempera and gold leaf on wood panel - Princeton University Art Museum - DSC06701
0816dc776ae6.read: A late Byzantine panel of the Twelve, painted in Greece in the early 1300s. They stand in a single rank, each holding a book or scroll. Matthew 10 is the chapter that names them and sends them out, and its warnings — sheep among wolves, councils, scourgings, betrayal by kindred — are the biography of every face on this panel.

890086731821.label: The Forerunner Led to Prison — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
890086731821.title: Elkomenos Prodromos Phylaken Dionysiou
890086731821.read: St John the Forerunner led away to prison — Dionysiou, Athos. The Greek titulus names the scene. It is from that prison that John sent his disciples to ask, Art thou he that should come? The greatest of those born of women is painted being dragged by a soldier, and asks a question.

12d1b6b5abd7.label: Christ Pantocrator — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
12d1b6b5abd7.title: Christos Pantokrator Dionysiou
12d1b6b5abd7.read: Christ Pantocrator in the dome of the katholikon at Dionysiou. He blesses with the right hand and holds the Gospel in the left, looking down on the whole church from the height. This is the face the Church raises over the words Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.

0b83261a7926.label: The Man with the Withered Hand — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
0b83261a7926.title: Iomenos xeran echon cheira Dionysiou
0b83261a7926.read: The healing of the man with the withered hand, in the synagogue on the sabbath — Dionysiou, Athos. The Pharisees sit on either side watching. Christ heals in front of them and asks the question the icon leaves hanging: is it lawful to do well on the sabbath days?

632d526875ab.label: The Deliverance of the Possessed — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
632d526875ab.title: Iomenos Daimonizomenous Dionysiou
632d526875ab.read: Christ casting out a devil, Dionysiou, Athos. The man stands stripped and bent; the spirit leaves him as a small dark shape. This is the healing after which the Pharisees said he cast out devils by Beelzebub — the moment Matthew places just before the warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.

74e4150f14a6.label: The Prophet Jonah — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
74e4150f14a6.title: Prophetes Ionas Ketos Dionysiou
74e4150f14a6.read: The prophet Jonah and the great fish, Dionysiou, Athos. Christ himself gave this as the only sign that would be given: as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale’s belly, so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. The Church reads the book of Jonah entire at the Paschal Vigil.

cc70160df0fc.label: The Theotokos Panachranta — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
cc70160df0fc.title: Theotokos Panachranta Dionysiou
cc70160df0fc.read: The Theotokos Panachranta — the All-Immaculate — from Dionysiou on Mount Athos. She is enthroned with the Child. The Church sets her image over the words Whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother: she is the first and the pattern of that obedience.

d3cd28ed2081.label: The Parable of the Sower — Orthodox mosaic
d3cd28ed2081.title: Representation of the Sower's parable
d3cd28ed2081.read: A modern Orthodox mosaic of the Sower — Pilda Semănătorului. The four grounds of Matthew 13 are laid out around the sowing Christ: the beaten path where the birds come, the stony place, the thorns, and the good earth. Christ is himself the Sower, and the seed is the word of the kingdom.
hot: The Sower
He that soweth the good seed is the Son of man. He is painted sowing broadcast, without measuring the ground — the word is given to every soil alike.
The birds on the wayside
Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. The path is beaten hard by traffic: a heart worn smooth by everything that passes over it.
The stony ground
He heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it; yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while. The stones lie just under a thin skin of earth.
The thorns and the good ground
The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word. Beyond them the green ground bears thirtyfold, sixtyfold, an hundredfold.

fd69652893db.label: The Beheading of the Forerunner — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
fd69652893db.title: Apotome Agiou Ioannou Prodromou Dionysiou
fd69652893db.read: The Beheading of the Forerunner, Dionysiou, Athos. The Church keeps this feast on the 29th of August as a strict fast — one of the few days of mourning in the calendar that is not for Christ himself. The icon shows both the executioner’s stroke and the head already on the charger.

8b7f7d9d5bf8.label: The Blessing of the Five Loaves — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
8b7f7d9d5bf8.title: Evlogesis Pente Arton Dionysiou
8b7f7d9d5bf8.read: The blessing of the five loaves — Dionysiou, Athos. Christ blesses, the disciples distribute, the multitude sits on the green grass, and the baskets of fragments stand in the foreground. He took, blessed, brake and gave: the four verbs of the Eucharist, which is why this icon is never far from the Mystical Supper.

eeb8331bcc9e.label: Christ Saving Peter from the Waves — Monreale, 12th c.
eeb8331bcc9e.title: Monreale - Peter Saved from the Waves
eeb8331bcc9e.read: Christ catching Peter as he begins to sink, from Monreale. The mosaic keeps the exact moment Matthew records — Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him. Peter is painted already half in the water: the icon is honest about how far he had got before the hand came.

bced617a4e30.label: The Canaanite Woman — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
bced617a4e30.title: Christos Iomenos Thygatera Xananaias Dionysiou
bced617a4e30.read: Christ and the Canaanite woman, Dionysiou, Athos. She kneels and will not be sent away; her daughter lies at home. Her answer — the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table — drew from Christ a word he said to no one else: O woman, great is thy faith.

d5a17108ebef.label: The Multiplication of the Loaves — Monreale, 12th c.
d5a17108ebef.title: Monreale - Multiplication of the Loaves and Fishes
d5a17108ebef.read: The multiplication of the loaves, from the Monreale mosaics. Christ blesses, the crowds are seated in ranks, and the baskets are gathered. Matthew records two such feedings; the second, of four thousand, follows the healings on the mountain, and the Fathers read the two together as the calling first of Israel and then of the nations.

0c81d57a20b0.label: The Transfiguration — Sinai, 12th c.
0c81d57a20b0.title: Transfiguration of Christ Icon Sinai 12th century
0c81d57a20b0.read: Christ stands in a mandorla of uncreated light on Mount Tabor. Moses and Elias — the Law and the Prophets — stand on either side, the dead and the living, both alive to him. Below, the three disciples are thrown down: Orthodox iconography always paints them falling, because the light of Tabor is not seen with the eyes but endured. St Gregory Palamas taught from this scene that the light of the Transfiguration is the uncreated energy of God himself, and that this same light is the inheritance of the saints.
hot: The mandorla of uncreated light

The almond of light around Christ is often painted darkening toward the centre. Divine light is not brightness added to Christ; it is the eternal glory that was always his, briefly shown to eyes that could not otherwise bear it.
Moses and Elias
Moses, who died and was buried, and Elias, who was taken up alive: the Law and the Prophets stand with him, and death and life are equally under his feet.
The disciples cast down
Peter, James and John fall with faces hidden or turned. They are painted in disorder while the upper register is perfectly still — the two orders of the icon are earth and heaven.

b5aeb19e98db.label: The Good Shepherd — Great Palace, Constantinople, 5th–6th c.
b5aeb19e98db.title: The Good Shepherd from the Imperial Palace of Constantinople 5th-6th century AD
b5aeb19e98db.read: A floor mosaic from the Great Palace of Constantinople, fifth or sixth century — one of the oldest Christian images of the shepherd. Before the Church painted Christ bearded and enthroned she painted him as a countryman with a flock. Doth he not leave the ninety and nine, and goeth into the mountains, and seeketh that which is gone astray?

18b841ec8665.label: The Labourers in the Vineyard — Byzantine Gospel book, 11th c.
18b841ec8665.title: Workers in the vineyard, Minuscule 269 (11th century)
18b841ec8665.read: A miniature from an eleventh-century Byzantine Gospel manuscript. The householder hires labourers at the gate in the upper register; in the lower they work the vines. The parable is the Church’s image for the vineyard passages of Matthew: the eleventh-hour labourer receives the same penny, and the last shall be first.

afa7c09513ff.label: The Blind Men of Jericho — Monreale, 12th c.
afa7c09513ff.title: Christ heals two Jericho blind men
afa7c09513ff.read: The two blind men of Jericho, from Monreale. They cry out over the crowd’s rebuke — Have mercy on us, O Lord, thou Son of David — and Christ stands still and touches their eyes. The Jesus Prayer of the Orthodox Church is built out of their words.

7cd490c6152f.label: The Entry into Jerusalem — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
7cd490c6152f.title: Baiophoros Dionysiou
7cd490c6152f.read: The Entry into Jerusalem — Palm Sunday, the feast the Greeks call Baiophoros, the Palm-bearing. Christ rides toward the city on a colt, the disciples following, the people coming out with branches, and children spreading their garments in the way. He rides not a war-horse but a borrowed foal, entering his own city as the meek King of Zechariah’s prophecy.
hot: Christ on the colt
He sits sideways, turned back toward the disciples rather than toward the acclaim ahead — the icon shows a King indifferent to his own triumph.
The palm tree
Branches are cut from the tree above; in a few days the same crowd will cry differently. The icon holds the shout of Hosanna and the coming Passion in one frame.
The people of the city
Jerusalem pours out through its gate. Matthew says all the city was moved, saying, Who is this?
The garments spread in the way
The people strewed their garments in the way. In the icon the small figures at the road are children — the ones whose praise Christ defends in the temple the next day.

61b829bb9d62.label: The Cleansing of the Temple — Rossano Gospels, 6th c.
61b829bb9d62.title: Rossano Gospels - Cleansing of the Temple
61b829bb9d62.read: The cleansing of the temple, from the Rossano Gospels — a sixth-century Greek codex on purple parchment, written in silver. Christ drives out the changers and overturns the tables. It is the one scene in the Gospels where he uses force, and it is used against commerce inside the house of prayer.

542679055fe0.label: The Cursing of the Fig Tree — Langadas, Greece, 19th c.
542679055fe0.title: 074 Cursing the fig tree Icon from Saint Paraskevi Church in Langadas
542679055fe0.read: The cursing of the fig tree, a nineteenth-century Greek icon from St Paraskevi in Langadas. The tree stands full of leaves and empty of fruit, and withers at a word. The Fathers read it as a parable acted rather than spoken: a show of religion with nothing under it cannot survive the Lord’s hunger for fruit.

769af079a9d9.label: The Wedding Feast — Dionisius, Ferapontov Monastery, 1502
769af079a9d9.title: Parable of the Wedding Feast 04-14
769af079a9d9.read: The parable of the wedding feast, painted by Dionisius at the Ferapontov Monastery in 1502 — the finest surviving Russian fresco cycle of its age. The tables are set and the servants go out into the highways. At the edge of the scene stands the man without a wedding garment, who came in and was cast out.

55b6d2c3f412.label: Christ in Glory, from the Last Judgment — Gračanica, 14th c.
55b6d2c3f412.title: Christ, last judgment, narthex, GRACANICA 7 D39A0936
55b6d2c3f412.read: Christ in glory, from the Last Judgment in the narthex of Gračanica. The narthex — the porch a worshipper passes through on the way in — is where the Orthodox Church habitually paints the Judgment, so that no one enters the nave without walking under it. Matthew 24 is its text: they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven.

d7585bf8fa5e.label: The Wise and Foolish Virgins — Rossano Gospels, 6th c.
d7585bf8fa5e.title: RossGospWiseFoolVirginsF4
d7585bf8fa5e.read: A leaf from the Rossano Gospels, a sixth-century Greek codex written in silver and gold on purple-dyed parchment — one of the oldest illustrated Gospel books in the world. Christ stands at the door with the wise virgins, whose lamps are lit; the foolish are shut outside in the dark, their lamps gone out.
hot: The wise with burning lamps
They took oil in their vessels with their lamps. The Fathers read the oil as mercy and the lamps as the virginity or the faith that mercy alone keeps burning.
Christ at the door
The Bridegroom receives them. In the Orthodox Holy Week this parable is sung at the Bridegroom services: Behold, the Bridegroom cometh at midnight.
The shut door
And the door was shut. The refusal is not arbitrary: the foolish went away to buy at the very moment when only what they already had could serve.
The foolish in the dark
They are painted on the far side of the door, against the purple night. Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour.

d4f530364ab1.label: The Separation of the Sheep and the Goats — Ravenna, 6th c.
d4f530364ab1.title: Separation of Sheep and Goats MET cdi24-144-4s1
d4f530364ab1.read: One of the oldest images of the Last Judgment in Christian art — a sixth-century mosaic from Sant’Apollinare Nuovo in Ravenna, made when Byzantine mosaicists worked in Italy. Christ, beardless in the early manner, sits between two angels and divides the flock: the sheep on his right hand, the goats on his left. Matthew 25 is the only place in the Gospels where the criterion of judgment is stated outright, and it is not doctrine but mercy: I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat.
hot: Christ the Judge
He is seated, not standing, and makes no gesture of wrath — only of division. In Orthodox theology the judgment is the same love met differently by those who have and have not learned to receive it.
The angel in red
The angel of the sheep, robed in the colour of divine life, stands at Christ’s right hand.
The angel in blue
The angel of the goats, in the colour of the created and the far side. The two angels frame the whole scene as the two possibilities of one human life.
The sheep on the right
Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.
The goats on the left
They too ask, Lord, when saw we thee an hungred? Neither side recognised him — the difference was in what they did, not in what they knew.

ffae81c9ac4b.label: Christ before Caiaphas — Gračanica, 14th c.
ffae81c9ac4b.title: Christ before Caiaphas, GRACANICA 1 090A7764
ffae81c9ac4b.read: Christ before Caiaphas, a fresco from Gračanica. The high priest is enthroned and the council sits about him; Christ stands bound and silent. Matthew opens the Passion with this council taking counsel to kill him by subtilty — and adds, but not on the feast day, which is precisely when it happened.

1700683b5e46.label: The Anointing at Bethany — Monreale, 12th c.
1700683b5e46.title: Monreale - Anointing at Bethany
1700683b5e46.read: The anointing at Bethany, from Monreale. The woman breaks the alabaster box over Christ’s head at table while the disciples object to the waste. She hath wrought a good work upon me: in that she hath poured this ointment on my body, she did it for my burial. The Orthodox Church sings of her through Holy Wednesday.

b9c2dc87cce1.label: Judas Receiving the Silver — Yaroslavl school, 19th c.
b9c2dc87cce1.title: Judas receiving money, icon of Yaroslavl (19 c, priv.coll)
b9c2dc87cce1.artist: Anonymous Russian icon painter (before 1917)Public domain image (according to PD-Russia-expired)
b9c2dc87cce1.read: Judas receiving the thirty pieces of silver — a nineteenth-century icon of the Yaroslavl school. The priests count out the money on the table. Thirty pieces was the price of a slave in the law of Moses, and Zechariah had already named the sum: a goodly price that I was prised at of them.

2f9b9ae9e6e4.label: The Mystical Supper — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
2f9b9ae9e6e4.title: Deipnos Mystikos Dionysiou
2f9b9ae9e6e4.read: The Mystical Supper is painted around a curved table so that no one has his back to the viewer — the Church is meant to see herself seated there. Christ presides; the beloved disciple leans toward his breast; and one hand reaches to the dish, the sign Christ gave of the betrayer. Matthew’s account is the one the Church reads on Holy Thursday: Take, eat; this is my body.
hot: Christ presiding
He is set at the head, larger than the rest, his hand raised in blessing over the bread. The Supper is painted not as a farewell meal but as the first Liturgy.
The beloved disciple
John leans toward the Lord’s breast — the posture the Fathers read as the model of prayer: the disciple who listens at the heart of Christ.
The common dish
He that dippeth his hand with me in the dish, the same shall betray me. The dish stands at the centre of the table, and Judas is known by his reach toward it, not by any mark of monstrosity.

7a949a6fedd9.label: Peter and the Cock — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
7a949a6fedd9.title: Alektor Petrou Dionysiou
7a949a6fedd9.read: Peter and the cock, Dionysiou, Athos. The scene is set in the high priest’s courtyard where Peter sat with the servants; the bird is painted small on a wall or roof. Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. The icon of the denial is also the icon of the tears that followed it.

51116569bee9.label: The Prayer in Gethsemane — Theophanes the Cretan, Stavronikita, 16th c.
51116569bee9.title: The Lord's prayer in Gethsemane - Stavronikita monastery, Mt Athos - Theophanes of Crete, 16th c.
51116569bee9.read: The prayer in Gethsemane, painted by Theophanes the Cretan at Stavronikita on Mount Athos in the sixteenth century — Theophanes is the master of the Cretan school and one of the great Orthodox iconographers. Christ prays alone on the rock while the three disciples sleep below. O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.

417a35d2ac73.label: The Betrayal — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
417a35d2ac73.title: Prodosia Dionysiou
417a35d2ac73.read: The Betrayal — Prodosia — from Dionysiou on Athos. Judas takes Christ by the shoulders to kiss him while the crowd closes in with swords and staves and torches; at the edge Peter strikes at Malchus. Friend, wherefore art thou come? The icon leaves Christ perfectly still at the centre of a scene made entirely of motion.

8e2957ac4beb.label: Christ Judged — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
8e2957ac4beb.title: Krinomenos Christou Dionysiou
8e2957ac4beb.read: Christ being judged, Dionysiou, Athos. He stands before the seated authority, bound, answering nothing. The composition is deliberately reversed from the icons of Christ enthroned: the Judge of all stands, and men sit above him.

e17a9e65d38f.label: Judas Returns the Thirty Pieces — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
e17a9e65d38f.title: Ypestrepseta Triakonta Argyria Ioudas
e17a9e65d38f.read: Judas returning the thirty pieces of silver — Dionysiou, Athos. He casts down the money in the temple; the priests refuse it. I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood. The Fathers distinguish his remorse sharply from Peter’s repentance: both wept, but only one went back to the Lord.

6023be53979c.label: Pilate Washing His Hands — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
6023be53979c.title: Aponepsis Pilatou Dionysiou
6023be53979c.read: Pilate washing his hands — Dionysiou, Athos. The governor is enthroned and a servant pours water over his fingers while Christ stands to one side. I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it. The icon fixes the moment a man performs a ritual of innocence in the act of committing the crime.

22a3d28c32fa.label: The Crucifixion — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
22a3d28c32fa.title: Stavrosis Dionysiou
22a3d28c32fa.read: The Orthodox Crucifixion is painted with restraint: Christ is not writhing but reigning from the tree. The body inclines but the face is at peace, because the icon shows a death freely given, not a defeat suffered. The Theotokos stands on his right and the beloved disciple on his left; the two thieves hang beside him, one turning toward him and one away.
hot: Christ reigning from the Cross
The head bows but the body is upright and composed. Orthodox iconography refuses to dwell on physical agony: what is shown is the voluntary self-offering of the Lord of glory.
The Theotokos
She stands at his right hand, the place of honour, receiving the word: Woman, behold thy son. The Church has always seen in her the first of those given to the beloved disciple’s care.
The two thieves
On either side hang the two crucified with him. Matthew records that both reviled him; the Church remembers that one repented, and made of the cross itself a door into paradise.

90bb6dd72243.label: The Lamentation at the Tomb — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
90bb6dd72243.title: Epitaphios Threnos Dionysiou
90bb6dd72243.read: The Lamentation at the Tomb — the Epitaphios Threnos of Holy Friday. Matthew tells it briefly: Joseph of Arimathaea begged the body, wrapped it in clean linen, and laid it in his own new tomb. The icon fills the silence with the mourning of the Church: the Theotokos holds her Son’s head against her face, the myrrhbearers raise their hands, and the empty cross stands behind against a night sky.
hot: The empty Cross
The instrument stands bare in the middle distance, the ladder still leaning against it. The work is finished; what remains is burial.
The Theotokos
She holds his head against her own — the same embrace many icons give the Mother and Child, now at the other end of the life. What began in the manger ends on the stone.
The stone of unction
The body lies wrapped on a red slab, anointed for burial. The same stone is venerated in Jerusalem, and every Orthodox altar keeps its memory in the antimension.
Joseph and Nicodemus
The two secret disciples come with the ladder and the linen. Matthew names Joseph of Arimathaea, a rich man, who dared to ask Pilate for the body.

d5b36ae3319a.label: The Sealed Tomb — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
d5b36ae3319a.title: Mnemeion Christou Dionysiou
d5b36ae3319a.read: The tomb of Christ — Dionysiou, Athos. The sealed sepulchre with its watch, from the end of Matthew 27. The chief priests asked for a guard lest the disciples steal him away; the Church has always noted that they thereby provided the Resurrection with impartial witnesses and made the stone’s seal part of the evidence.

c8cde9e68f3f.label: “Behold the Place Where the Lord Lay” — Dionysiou, Athos, 1547
c8cde9e68f3f.title: Ide Topos pou Ekato Dionysiou
c8cde9e68f3f.read: The inscription over the scene is the angel’s word in Matthew: Behold the place where the Lord lay. Orthodox iconography never paints the moment of the Resurrection itself — no one saw it — but only its evidence: an open tomb, folded grave-clothes, an angel sitting on the stone, and the women who came at dawn with spices.
hot: The myrrhbearing women
Mary Magdalene and the other Mary come with their spices. Matthew makes them the first witnesses and the first preachers of the Resurrection — sent by the angel to tell the apostles.
The angel on the stone
His countenance was like lightning, and his raiment white as snow. He sits upon the rolled-away stone: the seal of death is now a seat.
The empty grave-clothes
The tomb is shown open and orderly, the linen still lying in place. The body was not taken; it passed through.
The sleeping guard
The soldiers set to make the tomb sure lie as dead men. The precaution taken against the Resurrection became its unwilling witness.

user-nativity.label: The Nativity of Christ
user-nativity.title: The Nativity of Christ
user-nativity.read: The Orthodox Nativity is not a single moment but the whole mystery gathered into one field. The cave is black — the darkness of a world without God — and the Child lies in it bound like a corpse in a manger shaped like a tomb: the icon of the Nativity already contains the icon of the burial. Around the cave the whole creation brings its gift, as the hymn of the feast says: the angels their singing, the heavens a star, the magi their gifts, the shepherds their wonder, the earth a cave, and mankind a Virgin Mother.
hot: The single ray from the star

One ray descends from a single point of light and divides in three over the cave: the one God, the Holy Trinity, and the star that the Magi followed. The light comes from outside the created order — it is not painted as a source within the picture.
The Theotokos at the centre

She is the largest figure and lies at rest, not in the exhaustion of ordinary birth. In many Greek icons she turns away from the Child toward Joseph — toward the doubting world she is about to answer.
The manger like a tomb

The Child is wrapped in swaddling bands that are painted as grave-clothes and laid in a stone manger shaped as a sarcophagus. The ox and the ass stand over him, fulfilling Isaiah: the ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master’s crib.
Joseph and the old man

Joseph sits apart, troubled, while a bent old shepherd speaks to him — the tempter, who whispers that a virgin birth is impossible. This is Matthew’s Joseph, the just man who doubted before the angel came to him in the dream.
The washing of the Child
The midwives bathe the newborn: the icon insists on a real human infancy against every teaching that Christ only appeared to take flesh.

passages.name: The Genealogy of Christ
passages.subject: The Tree of Jesse / Genealogy of Christ
passages.keyText: The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.
passages.story: Matthew opens his gospel not with the birth but with the family tree: forty-two generations from Abraham to Christ, arranged in three equal spans of fourteen. The genealogy is a confession of faith — it declares that this child is the one the whole of Israel’s history was reaching toward. Four women appear by name: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and the wife of Uriah — all outsiders or sinners, signs from the very first line that the Messiah comes for all people.
notes: Three times fourteen
Three groups of fourteen generations: from Abraham to David, from David to the Exile, from the Exile to Christ — three epochs of salvation history, and Christ the goal of all three.
The four women
Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba — all outsiders or sinners by human reckoning, yet honoured in the genealogy of the Lord. Grace exceeds all human boundaries.
The name ‘Christ’
The list ends with ‘Jesus, who is called Christ.’ The whole of Israel was, unknowingly, praying for this name.

fathers.w: Hom. III, and Aug. City of God, 15, 15
fathers.t: Matthew then, desiring to preserve in memory the lineage of the Lord’s humanity through the succession of His parents, begins with Abraham, saying, "Abraham begat Isaac." Why does he not mention Ismael, his first-born? And again, "Isaac began Jacob;" why does he not speak of Esau his first-born? Because through them he could not have come down to David.

In the fourth book of Kings we read, that Ochozias was the son of Joram. On his death, Josabeth, sister of Ochozias and daughter of Joram, took Joash, her brother’s son, and preserved him from the slaughter of the royal seed by Athalias. To Joash succeeded his son Amasias; after him his son Azarias, who is called Ozias; after him his son Joatham. Thus you see according to historical truth there were three intervening kings, who are omitted by the Evangelist. Joram, moveover, begot not Ozias, but Ochozias, and the rest as we have related.

Let us not think this is to be overlooked, that though there were seventeen Kings of Judaea between David and Jeconiah, Matthew only recounts fourteen. We must observe that there might be many more successions to the throne than generations of men; for some may live longer and beget children later; or might be altogether without seed; thence the number of Kings and of generations would not coincide.

verses.t: The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.
Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren;
And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar; and Phares begat Esrom; and Esrom begat Aram;
And Aram begat Aminadab; and Aminadab begat Naasson; and Naasson begat Salmon;
And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth; and Obed begat Jesse;
And Jesse begat David the king; and David the king begat Solomon of her that had been the wife of Urias;
And Solomon begat Roboam; and Roboam begat Abia; and Abia begat Asa;
And Asa begat Josaphat; and Josaphat begat Joram; and Joram begat Ozias;
And Ozias begat Joatham; and Joatham begat Achaz; and Achaz begat Ezekias;
And Ezekias begat Manasses; and Manasses begat Amon; and Amon begat Josias;
And Josias begat Jechonias and his brethren, about the time they were carried away to Babylon:
And after they were brought to Babylon, Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel;
And Zorobabel begat Abiud; and Abiud begat Eliakim; and Eliakim begat Azor;
And Azor begat Sadoc; and Sadoc begat Achim; and Achim begat Eliud;
And Eliud begat Eleazar; and Eleazar begat Matthan; and Matthan begat Jacob;
And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ.

So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David until the carrying away into Babylon are fourteen generations; and from the carrying away into Babylon unto Christ are fourteen generations.

passages.name: The Nativity of Christ
passages.subject: The Nativity of Christ (Mt 1:18-25 is the Nativity Gospel)
passages.keyText: Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us.
passages.story: Matthew tells the Nativity from Joseph’s side. Before Mary and Joseph had come together she was found with child of the Holy Ghost; Joseph, being a just man, purposed to put her away privily. Then the angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream: fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife. The child was to be named Jesus — God saves — and Isaiah’s ancient word was fulfilled: Emmanuel, God with us. These are the verses the Orthodox Church reads as the Gospel of the Nativity.
notes: The angel in the dream
Joseph receives the annunciation not waking but in a dream: the divine word enters the stillness of the heart.
The name JESUS
Hebrew Yeshua: God saves. The name is not a decoration but a declaration of mission.
Emmanuel, God with us
Isaiah is fulfilled: God does not send a messenger but comes himself, and the humanity he takes is forever his own.

fathers.t: The Evangelist having said that she was found with child of the Holy Ghost, and without knowledge of man, that you should not herein suspect Christ’s disciple of inventing wonders in honour of his Master, brings forward Joseph confirming the history by his own share in it; "Now Joseph her husband, being a just man."

What will any one see in the Blessed Virgin more than in other mothers, if she be not the mother of God, but of Christ, or the Lord, as Nestorius says? For it would not be absurd should any one please to name the mother of any anointed person, the mother of Christ. Yet she alone and more than they is called the Holy Virgin, and the mother of Christ. For she bare not a simple man as ye say, but rather the Word incarnate, and made man of God the Father.

What is spoken to Ahaz then is to be thus understood. This Child, that shall be born of a Virgin of the house of David, shall now be called Emmanuel, that is, God with us, because the events (perhaps delivery from the two hostile kings) will make it appear that you have God present with you. But after He shall be called Jesus, that is, Saviour, because He shall save the whole human race. Wonder not, therefore, O house of David, at the newness of this thing, that a Virgin should bring forth a God, seeing He has so great might that though yet to be born after a long while, He delivers you now when you call upon Him.

verses.t: Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost.
Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily.

But while he thought on these things, behold, the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a dream, saying, Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost.
And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.
Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying,
Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us.
Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife:
And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS.

passages.name: Adoration of the Magi
passages.subject: The Adoration of the Magi
passages.keyText: And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him: and... presented unto him gifts; gold, and frankincense, and myrrh.
passages.story: Wise men from the East followed a rising star to Jerusalem, troubling Herod and all the city. Sent on to Bethlehem, they found the child with Mary his mother, fell down and worshipped him, and opened their treasures — gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went home another way.
notes: The moving star
A star that travels and stops over the cave: the heavens themselves announce the King, the first preachers of the gospel.
The three gifts
Gold, frankincense, and myrrh — confessing kingship, divinity, and the death to come.
The enthroned Mother
Mary is shown as a living throne, presenting the Child outward to the world; she is the Theotokos, the God-bearer.

fathers.t: Let Marcion and Paul of Samosata then blush, who will not see what the Magi saw, those progenitors of the Church adoring God in the flesh. That He was truly in the flesh, the swaddling clothes and the stall prove; yet that they worshipped Him not as mere man, but as God, the gifts prove which it was becoming to offer to a God. Let the Jews also be ashamed, seeing the Magi coming before them, and themselves not even earnest to tread in their path.

The following is the sense of the prophecy. Thou, Bethlehem, of the land of Judah, or Ephrata, (which is added to distinguish it from another Bethlehem in Galilee,) though thou art a small village among the thousand cities of Judah, yet out of thee shall be born Christ, who shall be the Ruler of Israel, who according to the flesh is of the seed of David, but was born of Me before the worlds; and therefore it is written, "His goings forth are of old. In the beginning was the Word."

After the miraculous Virgin-birth, a God-man having by Divine power proceeded from a virgin womb; in the obscure shelter of such a cradle, a narrow stall, wherein lay Infinite Majesty in a body more narrow, a God was suckled and suffered the wrapping of vile rags - amidst all this, on a sudden a new star shone in the sky upon the earth, and driving away the darkness of the world, changed night into day; that the day-star should not be hidden by the night.

verses.t: Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem,
Saying, Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him.
When Herod the king had heard these things, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.
And when he had gathered all the chief priests and scribes of the people together, he demanded of them where Christ should be born.
And they said unto him, In Bethlehem of Judaea: for thus it is written by the prophet,
And thou Bethlehem, in the land of Juda, art not the least among the princes of Juda: for out of thee shall come a Governor, that shall rule my people Israel.
Then Herod, when he had privily called the wise men, enquired of them diligently what time the star appeared.
And he sent them to Bethlehem, and said, Go and search diligently for the young child; and when ye have found him, bring me word again, that I may come and worship him also.
When they had heard the king, they departed; and, lo, the star, which they saw in the east, went before them, till it came and stood over where the young child was.
When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy.

And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him: and when they had opened their treasures, they presented unto him gifts; gold, and frankincense, and myrrh.
And being warned of God in a dream that they should not return to Herod, they departed into their own country another way.

passages.name: The Flight into Egypt
passages.subject: The Flight into Egypt
passages.keyText: And was there until the death of Herod: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Out of Egypt have I called my son.
passages.story: After the Magi departed an angel warned Joseph in a dream: arise, take the young child and his mother and flee into Egypt, for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him. They went by night. The Lord who would one day lead his people out of Egypt is himself carried down into it as a refugee, and Hosea’s word is fulfilled: Out of Egypt have I called my son.

fathers.t: See how immediately on His birth the tyrant is furious against Him, and the mother with her Child is driven into foreign lands. So should you in the beginning of your spiritual career seem to have tribulation, you need not to be discouraged, but bear all things manfully, having this example.

Let those who deny the authenticity of the Hebrew copies, shew us this passage in the LXX, and when they have failed to find it, we will shew it them in the Hebrew. We may also explain it in another way, by considering it as quoted from Numbers, "God brought him out of Egypt; his glory is as it were that of a unicorn."

The first time when he would teach Joseph that she was lawfully espoused, the Angel called the Virgin his espoused "wife;" but after the birth she is only spoken of as the Mother of Jesus. As wedlock was rightfully imputed to her in her virginity, so virginity is esteemed venerable in her as the mother of Jesus.

verses.t: And when they were departed, behold, the angel of the Lord appeareth to Joseph in a dream, saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be thou there until I bring thee word: for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him.
When he arose, he took the young child and his mother by night, and departed into Egypt:
And was there until the death of Herod: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Out of Egypt have I called my son.

passages.name: The Holy Innocents of Bethlehem
passages.subject: The Holy Innocents of Bethlehem
passages.keyText: In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.
passages.story: Herod, seeing that the wise men had not returned to him, sent and slew all the children in Bethlehem from two years old and under. Jeremiah’s lament was fulfilled: Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not. The Church honours these children as the first martyrs of Christ — witnesses who suffered for him before they could speak his name.

fathers.t: The Evangelist by this history of so bloody a massacre, having filled the reader with horror, now again sooths his feelings, shewing that these things were not done because God could not hinder, or knew not of them; but as the Prophet had foretold.

O blessed infants! He only will doubt of your crown in this your passion for Christ, who doubts that the baptism of Christ has a benefit for infants. He who at His birth had Angels to proclaim Him, the heavens to testify, and Magi to worship Him, could surely have prevented that these should not have died for Him, had He not known that they died not in that death, but rather lived in higher bliss. Far be the thought, that Christ who came to set men free, did nothing to reward those who died in His behalf, when hanging on the cross He prayed for those who put Him to death.

Rachel’s son was Benjamin, in which tribe Bethlehem is not situated. How then does Rachel weep for the children of Judah as if they were her own? We answer briefly. She was buried near Bethlehem in Ephrata, and was regarded as the mother, because her body was there entertained. Or, as the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin were contiguous, and Herod’s command extended to the coasts of Bethlehem as well as to the town itself, we may suppose that many were slain in Benjamin.

verses.t: Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth, and sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently enquired of the wise men.
Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying,
In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.

passages.name: The Return to Nazareth
passages.subject: The Return from Egypt / Christ dwells in Nazareth
passages.keyText: And he came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophets, He shall be called a Nazarene.
passages.story: When Herod was dead the angel appeared again to Joseph in Egypt and bade him take the young child and his mother back into the land of Israel. Hearing that Archelaus reigned in Judaea in his father’s room, Joseph turned aside into Galilee and settled in Nazareth — an obscure town of no reputation — so that the word of the prophets should be fulfilled, He shall be called a Nazarene. The hidden years begin here.
notes: The cave and the star
Not a palace but a cave: Christ enters the darkest place to fill it with light. The star sends its ray straight down, joining heaven and earth.
The Holy Innocents
The slaughter of the innocents is part of the Nativity story: the powers of the world rage against the King they cannot control.
The Holy Family on the road
Joseph leads Mary and the child into Egypt by night: the Lord of all becomes a refugee, sharing the road of the hunted.

fathers.t: And when he had once left the country of His birth, all the occurrences passed out of mind; the rage of persecution had been spent in Bethlehem and its neighbourhood. By choosing Nazareth therefore, Joseph both avoided danger, and returned to his country.

The whole of this history, from the account of the Magi inclusively, Luke omits. Let it be here noticed once for all, that each of the Evangelists writes as if he were giving a full and complete history, which omits nothing; where he really passes over any thing, he continues his thread of history as if he had told all. Yet by a diligent comparison of their several narratives, we can be at no loss to know where to insert any particular that is mentioned by one and not by the other.

Many here err from ignorance of history, supposing the Herod who mocked our Lord on the day of His passion, and the Herod whose death is here related, were the same. But the Herod who was then made friends with Pilate was son of this Herod and brother to Archelaus; for Archelaus was banished to Lyons in Gaul, and his father Herod made king in his room, as we read in Josephus.

verses.t: But when Herod was dead, behold, an angel of the Lord appeareth in a dream to Joseph in Egypt,
Saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel: for they are dead which sought the young child’s life.
And he arose, and took the young child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel.

But when he heard that Archelaus did reign in Judaea in the room of his father Herod, he was afraid to go thither: notwithstanding, being warned of God in a dream, he turned aside into the parts of Galilee:
And he came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophets, He shall be called a Nazarene.

passages.name: St John the Forerunner
passages.subject: St John the Forerunner preaching in the wilderness
passages.keyText: The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
passages.story: John the Baptist appeared in the wilderness of Judaea, clothed in camel’s hair, his food locusts and wild honey, preaching repentance and the nearness of the kingdom. Jerusalem and all Judaea came to be baptized in the Jordan, confessing their sins. He warned of the wrath to come, and pointed beyond himself to One mightier, whose sandal he was not worthy to carry.
notes: The angel’s wings
John is given wings because ‘angel’ means messenger: he is the herald sent before the face of Christ.
The axe at the root
An axe laid to the foot of a tree: a summons to bear the fruit of repentance, not merely profess faith.
Camel’s hair and girdle
His rough garment marks the ascetic and prophet: he belongs not to the palace but wholly to God.

fathers.t: For while as yet the sacrifice had not been offered, nor remission of sin sent, nor the Spirit had descended on the water, how could sin be forgiven? But since the Jews never perceived their own sin, and this was the cause of all their evils, John came to bring them to a sense of them by calling them to repentance.

The preacher of Christ is clad in the skins of unclean beasts, to which the Gentiles are compared, and so by the Prophets’ dress is sanctified whatever in them was useless or unclean. The girdle is a thing of much efficacy to every good work, that we may be girt for every ministry of Christ. For his food are chosen locusts, which fly the face of man, and escape from every approach, signifying ourselves who were borne away from every word or speech of good by a spontaneous motion of the body, weak in will, barren in works, fretful in speech, foreign in abode, are now become the food of the Saints, chosen to fill the Prophets’ desire, furnishing our most sweet food not from the hives of the law, but from the trunks of wild trees.

The other Evangelists omit these words of John. What follows, "This is He, &c." it is not clear whether the Evangelist speaks them in his own person, or whether they are part of John’s preaching, and the whole from "Repent ye," to "Esaias the prophet," is to be assigned to John. It is of no importance that he says, "This is he," and not, "I am he;" for Matthew speaking of himself says, "He found a man sitting at the toll-office;" not "He found me." Though when asked what he said of himself, he answered, as is related by John the Evangelist, "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness."

verses.t: In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judaea,
And saying, Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
And the same John had his raiment of camel’s hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins; and his meat was locusts and wild honey.
Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judaea, and all the region round about Jordan,
And were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their sins.
But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees come to his baptism, he said unto them, O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance:
And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.
And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.
I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:
Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.

passages.name: The Baptism of Christ
passages.subject: The Theophany / Baptism of Christ
passages.keyText: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
passages.story: Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John, who at first refused. As he came up from the water, the heavens opened; the Spirit descended like a dove; and the Father’s voice was heard: ‘This is my beloved Son.’ The feast is named Theophany — the showing-forth of God — for here the Holy Trinity is revealed.
notes: The dark water
The Jordan is painted almost as a watery abyss: Christ’s descent foreshadows his descent into death and the drowning of sin.
The dove and the ray
The Spirit descends as a dove upon a ray from the opened heavens, completing the revelation of the Holy Trinity.
Angels with veiled hands
Angels stand on the bank, hands covered in cloth: even the highest beings stand in awe at the mystery.

fathers.t: Because after his baptism Christ was to put an end to the Law, He therefore came to be baptized at this age, that having so kept the Law, it might not be said that He cancelled it, because He could not observe it.

Here are deeds of the whole Trinity. In their own substance indeed Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are One without interval of either place or time; but in my mouth they are three separate words, and cannot be pronounced at the same time, and in written letters they fill each their several places. By this comparison may be understood how the Trinity in Itself indivisible may be manifested dividedly in the likeness of a visible creation. That the voice is that of the Father only is manifest from the words, "This is my Son."

Scripture tells of many wonders wrought at various times in this river; as that, among others, in the Psalms, "Jordan was driven backwards;" before the water was driven back, now sins are turned back in its current; as Elijah divided the waters of old, so Christ the Lord wrought in the same Jordan the separation of sin.

verses.t: Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him.
But John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?
And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him.
And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:
And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.

passages.name: The Temptation of Christ
passages.subject: The Temptation of Christ in the wilderness
passages.keyText: Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
passages.story: After his baptism, Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness and fasted forty days. The devil tempted him three times — to turn stones to bread, to cast himself from the Temple, to gain the world’s kingdoms by worship. Each time Jesus answered with Scripture; at the third refusal the devil departed and angels ministered to him.
notes: The barren wilderness
Bare rock and emptiness: the place where there is nothing but God and the soul, and the contest is fought and won.
The tempter, small and dark
The devil is shown diminished before the Word made flesh: his power is real, but before Christ already broken.
The ministering angels
After the temptations are refused, the angels draw near to serve: the reward shown to all who endure.

fathers.t: Whoever thou art then that after thy baptism sufferest grievous trials, be not troubled thereat; for this thou receivedst arms, to fight, not to sit idle. God does not hold all trial from us; first, that we may feel that we are become stronger; secondly, that we may not be puffed up by the greatness of the gifts we have received; thirdly, that the Devil may have experience that we have entirely renounced him; fourthly, that by it we may be made stronger; fifthly, that we may receive a sign of the treasure entrusted to us; for the Devil would not come upon us to tempt us, did he not see us advanced to greater honours.

Not however because Christ fasted immediately after having received baptism, are we to suppose that He established a rule to be observed, that we should fast immediately after His baptism. But when the conflict with the tempter is sore, then we ought to fast, that the body may fulfil its warfare by chastisement, and the soul obtain victory by humiliation.

The Devil and Peter are not, as many suppose, condemned to the same sentence. To Peter it is said, "Get thee behind me, Satan;" i.e. follow thou behind Me who art contrary to My will. But here it is, "Go, Satan," and is not added, behind Me,’ that we may understand "into the fire prepared for thee and thy angels."

verses.t: Then was Jesus led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil.
And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred.
And when the tempter came to him, he said, If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread.
But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
Then the devil taketh him up into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple,

And saith unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone.
Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.
Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them;
And saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me.
Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.
Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him.

passages.name: Jesus Begins to Preach
passages.subject: Christ begins to preach (Christ the Teacher)
passages.keyText: From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
passages.story: Hearing that John was cast into prison, Jesus withdrew into Galilee and dwelt in Capernaum, upon the sea coast, in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim — the region Isaiah had called the land of the shadow of death, upon which a great light should shine. From that time he began to preach with the Forerunner’s own words: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.

fathers.t: But that you may learn that he speaks not of natural day and night, he calls the light, "a great light," which is in other places called "the true light;" and he adds, "the shadow of death," to explain what he means by darkness. The words "arose," and "shined," shew, that they found it not of their own seeking, but God Himself appeared to them, they did not first run to the light; for men were in the greatest miseries before Christ’s coming; they did not walk but safe in darkness; which was a sign that they hoped for deliverance; for as not knowing what way they should go, shut in by darkness they sat down, having now no power to stand. By darkness he means here, error and ungodliness.

John relates in his Gospel the calling of Peter, Andrew, and Nathanael, and the miracle of Cana, before Jesus’ departure into Galilee; all these things the other Evangelists have omitted, carrying on the thread of their narrative with Jesus’ return into Galilee. We must understand then that some days intervened, during which the things took place concerning the calling of the disciples which John relates.

They are said at the first time to be lightened from the burden of sin, because in the country of these two tribes, the Saviour first preached the Gospel; "at the last time" their faith "was increased," most of the Jews remaining in error.

verses.t: Now when Jesus had heard that John was cast into prison, he departed into Galilee;
And leaving Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum, which is upon the sea coast, in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim:
That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying,
The land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephthalim, by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles;
The people which sat in darkness saw great light; and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up.
From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.

passages.name: The Calling of the Fishermen
passages.subject: The Calling of Peter and Andrew, James and John
passages.keyText: Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.
passages.story: Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw Simon called Peter and Andrew casting their net, and called them. Immediately they left their nets and followed. Going further he saw James and John with their father mending nets; he called them also, and at once they left boat and father and followed.
notes: The net and boat
The tools of their former life left at once: the very moment of the great leaving, an image of conversion.
Christ’s outstretched hand
The Lord stands on the land and calls across the water: the gesture of calling that goes out to every generation.
Andrew the First-called
Andrew, the first to follow, is honoured as Protokletos — the First-called — the pattern of all who leave all to follow.

fathers.t: He made no promise to them when He called them, as He had to the former, for the obedience of the first had made the way plain for them. Besides, they had heard many things concerning Him, as being friends and townsmen of the others.

Had one learned been chosen, he might have attributed the choice to the merit of his learning. But our Lord Jesus Christ, willing to bow the necks of the proud, sought not to gain fishermen by orators, but gained an Emperor by a fisherman. Great was Cyprian the pleader, but Peter the fisherman was before him.

By this that they left their occupation and their father’s house we are taught, that when we would follow Christ we should not be holden of the cares of secular life, or of the society of the paternal mansion.

verses.t: And Jesus, walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brethren, Simon called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea: for they were fishers.
And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.
And they straightway left their nets, and followed him.
And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them.
And they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him.

passages.name: Jesus Heals the Multitudes
passages.subject: Christ healing the multitudes
passages.keyText: And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness and all manner of disease among the people.
passages.story: Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness among the people. They brought him all that were sick with divers diseases, those possessed with devils, the lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them. Great multitudes followed him from Galilee, Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judaea and beyond Jordan.

fathers.t: Observe the reserve of the Evangelist; he does not give an account of any one of the various cases of healing, but passes in one brief phrase an abundance of miracles, "they brought to him all their sick."

Not really smitten by the moon, but who were believed to be so through the subtlety of the daemons, who by observing the seasons of the moon, sought to bring an evil report against the creature, that is might redound to the blasphemy of the Creator.

Daemons are enticed to take up their abode in many creatures, (created not by themselves but God,) by delights adapted to their various natures; not that they are animals, drawn by meats; but spirits attracted by signs which agree with each one’s taste.

verses.t: And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness and all manner of disease among the people.

And his fame went throughout all Syria: and they brought unto him all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments, and those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them.
And there followed him great multitudes of people from Galilee, and from Decapolis, and from Jerusalem, and from Judaea, and from beyond Jordan.

passages.name: The Sermon on the Mount
passages.subject: The Sermon on the Mount / The Beatitudes
passages.keyText: Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
passages.story: Seeing the multitudes, Jesus went up into a mountain and taught them the Beatitudes — blessing the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and the persecuted. He named his disciples the salt of the earth and the light of the world.
notes: The mountain
Christ teaches from a mountain as Moses received the Law on Sinai: the new Law of the Beatitudes is given by God himself.
The hand raised in blessing
The teaching gesture of Christ is also a blessing: his words do not merely instruct but bestow the blessedness they name.
Salt and light
‘Ye are the salt of the earth... the light of the world.’ The disciples are sent to season and illumine all the nations.

fathers.t: We may remark that this blessing is given not simply, but with great force and emphasis; it is not simply, who have grief,’ but "who mourn." And indeed this command is the sum of all philosophy. For if they who mourn for the death of children or kinsfolk, throughout all that season of their sorrow, are touched with no other desires, as of money, or honour, burn not with envy, feel not wrongs, nor are open to any other vicious passion, but are solely given up to their grief; much more ought they, who mourn their own sins in such manner as they ought to mourn for them, to shew this higher philosophy.

The peacemakers within themselves are they who having stilled all disturbances of their spirits, having subjected them to reason, have overcome their carnal desires, and become the kingdom of God. There all things are so disposed, that that which is most chief and excellent in man, governs those parts which we have in common with the brutes, though they struggle against it; nay even that in man which is excellent is subjected to a yet greater, namely, the very Truth, the Son of God. For it would not be able to govern what is inferior to it, if it were not subject to what is above it. And this is the peace which is given on earth to men of good will.

Some of the less learned brethren suppose the Lord to have spoken what follows from the Mount of Olives, which is by no means the case; what went before and what follows fixes the place in Galilee - Mount Tabor, [ed. note: Mount Tabor is asserted by the Fathers and by tradition coming down to the present day to be the scene of the Transfiguration. But S. Jerome seems to be the only author who speaks of it as the scene of the Sermon on the Mount. The mount of the Beatitudes according to modern travellers lies near to Capernaum, and ten miles north of Mount Tabor. See Grewell Diss. vol. ii. 294. Pococke’s Descrip. of the East, vol. ii. 67] we may suppose, or any other high mountain.

verses.t: And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him:
And he opened his mouth, and taught them, saying,
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.
Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.
Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.
Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.
Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
